title: Remember now your creator (Ecclesiastes 12:1–8)
hook: before the silver cord is loosed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher found something that holds, and your line was a threefold cord. Did you thank the friend who lifted you? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

A big old house, at the end of a day. The guards at the door have started to tremble. The strong men are stooped. The women who grind the grain have stopped, because there are too few of them left. The ones who look out of the windows find everything dim. The doors to the street are shut, and the sound of the mill is low. Someone wakes at the first chirp of a bird. The almond tree is in bloom, all white. It sounds like a ghost story. It's actually a riddle, and the Preacher expects you to solve it. He's describing a body growing old. Today, the closing poem of his book.
screen: `A HOUSE AT THE END OF THE DAY.` → `THE GRINDERS CEASE.` → `IT'S A RIDDLE.` → `A BODY GROWING OLD.`

segments.voice: The poem opens, in the King James Bible: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them." Then comes the riddle of the house. One old way of reading decodes it like this. The keepers of the house who tremble are the hands and arms. The strong men bowing are the legs and back. The grinders that cease because they are few are the teeth. Those who look out of the windows are the eyes. Waking at the sound of a bird is light sleep in old age. And the almond tree in white blossom is white hair. Not every reader takes each image the same way, and some hear a whole town falling into ruin as well as a body. But the point lands either way. Then the images turn to endings: "Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken." A lamp hanging on a silver chain, the chain snaps, the golden bowl of oil shatters, the light goes out. A pitcher breaks at the well. And then: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." Now go back to the first word, remember. In Hebrew it's not only recalling a fact. It means to keep someone in mind and act on it, the way God remembers Noah in the flood and sends the wind. So remember your Creator isn't nostalgia. It's: live toward God now, while your hands are steady and your eyes are clear. The Preacher isn't trying to frighten the young. He's urging them not to wait.
screen: `REMEMBER, IN THE DAYS OF YOUTH.` · `A RIDDLE: HANDS, TEETH, EYES, HAIR.` · `THE SILVER CORD, THE GOLDEN BOWL.` · `REMEMBER MEANS ACT ON IT.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT SHALL RETURN UNTO GOD WHO GAVE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you can still do, today. Settle, and breathe. Feel your hands. Open and close them slowly. Notice your eyes taking in light, your ears catching small sounds. Whatever your age, there are things your body can do right now that it may not always do. Then let the Preacher's first word land: remember. The poem ends with the spirit returning to God who gave it. If you pray, you can offer today's strength back to the One who gave it. If you don't, simply hold the thought that this strength is here now, and not forever. The bell holds the time.
Remember now your creator. The Preacher's last poem: keep God in mind and act on it while you're young, before the silver cord is loosed.

Your line: remember, while you're young. Whatever your age, you're younger today than you'll ever be again. Use your strength on purpose once today: take the stairs, carry something for someone, walk the long way, and notice it as a gift while you have it. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 457 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOVE AS STRONG AS DEATH.`

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 12 is read at some Christian funerals, especially for older people, and its opening verse is often taught to young people in churches and youth groups as a call not to put faith off until later.

original.note: Hebrew: remember. in the Bible, remembering usually leads to acting.

trapdoor: what you thought: remember God means think about God sometimes.
what it means: keep God in mind and live toward him now, before age and death arrive.
what a scholar hears: zakhar, remember, often means to act on behalf of someone. and the Talmud already reads the riddle of the house as a body growing old.

notes: Editor pass (y2 review): hook no longer opens with 'Picture'; 'many readers, ancient and modern' softened to 'one old way of reading'; practice and carry no longer repeat day 451's 'do the thing you've been putting off' and now stay with the body and its gifts; trapdoor claim narrowed to the Talmud (Shabbat 151b–152a; confirm).

The decoding of 12:3–5 (keepers = hands/arms, strong men = legs, grinders = teeth, windows = eyes, almond blossom = white hair) is the traditional allegorical reading; the script says 'many readers' and notes other readings (a town in decline, a storm). Confirm.
Trapdoor claims the aging reading goes back to the Talmud (Shabbat 151b–152a) and early Christian writers; confirm the reference.
Silver cord / golden bowl as a hanging lamp: a common interpretation; confirm.
'Remember' (zakhar) as action-oriented, with Genesis 8:1 as the example. Confirm this isn't overstated.
